features.claim: Amargasaurus had a long tail and neck, a small head, and a barrel-shaped trunk.
features.quote: It followed the typical sauropod body plan, with a long tail and neck, a small head, and a barrel-shaped trunk supported by four column-like legs.
Amargasaurus was quadrupedal (moved on four legs), and probably was unable to rear on its hind legs.

features.claim: Amargasaurus had two parallel rows of tall spines down its neck and back.
features.quote: Most distinctively, it sported two parallel rows of tall spines down its neck and back, taller than in any other known sauropod.

features.claim: The spines on the neck were bowed backward and stuck up above the vertebra behind them.
features.quote: On the neck, they were bowed backward, projecting above the adjacent vertebra.

features.claim: The spines on the last two back vertebrae, the hip, and the front of the tail flared into a paddle shape at the top.
features.quote: The last two dorsal vertebrae, the hip, and the foremost tail in Amargasaurus also had elongated spines; these were not bifurcated but flared into a paddle-shaped upper end.

features.claim: Amargasaurus had a long, low skull on the end of a long neck.
features.quote: It was a quadrupedal herbivore with a long, low skull on the end of a long neck, much like its relative Dicraeosaurus.

features.claim: The nostril opening was in the back half of the skull, above and to the side of the eye opening.
features.quote: As in other dicraeosaurids, the external naris (nostril opening) was situated in the posterior half of the skull, diagonally above the orbit (eye opening), which was proportionally large.

features.claim: The forelimbs were a little shorter than the hind limbs.
features.quote: The forelimbs were somewhat shorter than the hind limbs, as in related sauropods.

features.claim: Amargasaurus probably had five digits on each hand and foot.
features.quote: Most of the hand and foot bones were not preserved, but Amargasaurus probably possessed five digits each as in all sauropods.

features.claim: Amargasaurus was small for a sauropod, about 9 to 13 meters long.
features.quote: Amargasaurus was small for a sauropod, measuring 9 to 13 meters (30 to 43 feet) in length and weighing approximately 2.5–4 metric tons (2.8–4.4 short tons).

not_this.claim: Old pictures showing the spines covered by a horn sheath are wrong; the spines were connected by ligaments instead.
not_this.quote: In 2022, a study by Ignacio Cerda and colleagues analyzing the external and internal bone structure of the spines of Amargasaurus and an indeterminate dicraeosaurid (also from the La Amarga Formation) suggested that the spines did not support a keratinous sheath as previously believed.

not_this.claim: Old pictures showing the head held nearly horizontal are wrong, because that posture would not have been possible.
not_this.quote: The first skeletal reconstructions show the skull in a near-horizontal posture. Salgado, in 1999, argued that such a posture would have been anatomically impossible due to the elongated neural spines of the neck vertebrae.

debated.claim: What the tall spines looked like in life and what they were for is still not settled.
debated.quote: Both the function and the appearance in life of the extremely elongated and bifurcated vertebral spines remain elusive.

debated.claim: One idea is that the spines held up two parallel skin sails.
debated.quote: Some subsequently published life restorations showed the double row of spines supporting two parallel skin sails.

debated.claim: Another idea is that the spines supported a single sail-like structure.
debated.quote: Another idea is that they supported a sail-like structure.

debated.claim: One suggestion is that the spines were covered by a horn sheath that made them longer.
debated.quote: Instead, he found that this shape indicates that the spines supported a keratinous (horn) sheath that would have extended the length of the spines in life.

second_reading.claim: Amargasaurus had teeth for grinding and chewing tough plants.
second_reading.quote:
Teeth:
teeth for grinding and chewing

second_reading.claim: The idea that Amargasaurus was a slow walker is wrong; it could move quickly.
second_reading.quote: This was contradicted by Gerardo Mazzetta and Richard Fariña in 1999, who argued that Amargasaurus was capable of rapid locomotion.
